sections.h2: What This Guide Covers
paras: This guide walks the photo half of the workspace: what the five image tools make, what one product photo can cover, and the checks that keep a generated photo safe to publish. By the end you'll know which tool fills which slot on your listing, what a photo costs, and what to look at before it goes live.

sections.h2: One Photo Starts the Whole Set

img.alt: Hands place your tan handbag upright on a pale studio surface for the catalog shot.

paras: Open the AI Image tool in your workspace, upload one photo of your product, and describe the shot you want. The generator keeps the shape, the color and the visible details from your reference photo, then places the product in the scene you described.

Every image costs 24 credits, and the exact cost shows before the job starts. If a job fails, the credits go back to your balance. The same photo can run through a different scene in the next minute — no booking, no props, no reshoot.

sections.h2: Five Photo Tools Cover a Full Listing

img.alt: A hand lifts your tan handbag from a softly lit cafe table so you can post that use shot.

paras: The workspace groups product images into five tools. [White background photos](/ai-image-generation/white-background-photos) give you the clean main image marketplaces expect. [Lifestyle photos](/ai-image-generation/lifestyle-photos) place the product in a real scene — a cafe table, a kitchen counter, a desk by the window. [Model photos](/ai-image-generation/model-photos) put clothes and accessories on a reusable AI model, and [social ad photos](/ai-image-generation/social-ad-photos) style images for Facebook and Instagram placements. Start with whichever photo your listing is missing today; the same product photo feeds all five.

sections.h2: Make a Product Photo in Three Steps
paras: Upload one clear photo of your product — daylight, plain background, shot from the front works best. Describe the scene in one or two sentences: the setting, the light, what sits around the product. Pick the size: square for product pages, 9:16 for stories, 16:9 for banners.

The cost appears before you confirm the job. Download the finished image, check it against the real product, then publish. If the first version is not right, change one line of the description and run it again — a rerun costs minutes, not a shoot.

sections.h2: Scenes the Generator Can Build

img.alt: A hand sets your tan handbag beside a folded scarf on the entry table, ready to post.

The reference photo anchors the product. If the generated product drifts — the label shifts, the color changes, the shape rounds off — drop that version and rerun with a clearer reference photo. A scene that hides the product is a scene that fails the listing.

mainEntity.name: How long does the pre-publish check take?

acceptedAnswer.text: About five minutes for a 15-second ad: watch it once on a phone, compare the product, read the subtitles, confirm rights and labels.

mainEntity.name: The product looks slightly off — publish or rerun?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rerun. An ad must match the product customers receive. A clearer reference photo and a sharper description usually fix it in one run.

mainEntity.name: The label text is unreadable — what do I do?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rerun the scene with a sharper reference photo, or frame the shot so the label is not the focus. Never publish wrong product text.

mainEntity.name: Can I edit the video after download?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes for words: Subtitle Studio burns in captions and promo lines on the finished file. Scene fixes need a regeneration of that scene.

mainEntity.name: Who owns the finished ad?

acceptedAnswer.text: You do. Files come without a watermark and are yours to run commercially, within the content policy.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to label AI content?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow each platform's current rules. Two constants: never present a generated face as a real buyer or reviewer, and never promise outcomes the product doesn't have.

mainEntity.name: What music can I use?

acceptedAnswer.text: The built-in library or tracks you have licensed. Don't drop in commercial songs you haven't cleared for ads.

mainEntity.name: Who types the price and the discount code?

sections.h2: What This Guide Covers
paras: This guide is the pre-publish pass for AI video ads: what to look at, in what order, and what to do when something is off. Two real clips generated on this site show exactly where accuracy problems hide — in the close-up details and in the promise the clip makes.
Run it as a list at the end; the whole pass takes about five minutes on a 15-second ad.

sections.h2: Why Every AI Ad Gets a Final Check

img.alt: Hands check the front pocket and zipper of plain black travel backpack.

paras: An AI workspace lets you produce ads at the speed you used to save for one shoot a quarter. Speed cuts both ways: the same afternoon can ship five versions, and the check decides which of them deserve your audience.
The workspace already gates two steps — you review the storyboard before the job runs, and the file before download. This checklist covers the last five minutes between download and publish.

sections.h2: Check the Product First

img.alt: Hands count pockets, buckles and straps on plain black travel backpack.

paras: Put the real product next to your screen. Compare the color in daylight, count the visible parts, and read every letter on the label — small text is where generation drifts first. If the label is wrong, fix the reference photo or the description and rerun.
Hands deserve a second look: check the grip, the proportions, and whatever the presenter does with the product. One clear action per clip is easier to verify than three.

sections.h2: Check the Close-Up Details
paras: Close-ups reward scrutiny. This example is built around a fabric-and-print close-up, which makes it the perfect practice clip: at this zoom you can see whether the print sits where it sits on the real garment, whether the texture reads true, and whether anything drifted.

video.alt: A second bedroom session with the washed-graphic cotton tee, this time lingering on the faded sunset print and the softness of the washed cotton.
video.label: Washed Graphic Tee Fabric Close-Up
video.caption: Real example: the close-up is where accuracy lives. Watch the print placement and the fabric texture — this is the level of detail to compare against the real product before you publish.

sections.h2: Check the Motion and the Voice

img.alt: Hands open the zipper and flap of plain black travel backpack.

paras: Watch the clip on a phone at full volume before you watch it anywhere else — that is where your audience meets it. Listen to the voiceover while reading the subtitles line by line: the spoken words and the burned-in text must match.
If the voice lands but one scene is off, you don't need to start over — regenerate the one scene, or keep the file and fix the words in [Subtitle Studio](/app/create/subtitles).

sections.h2: Check the Words You Typed Yourself

img.alt: Plain black travel backpack centered on a white background.

paras: Prices, dates, discount codes and shipping claims are yours to type. Add them in the caption or in Subtitle Studio — not as text you asked the generator to draw, because generated letters break and misread. A discount code that reads wrong costs more than any reshoot ever did.

sections.h2: Check the Claim the Clip Makes
paras: If the ad promises a difference, the difference has to happen on camera. Before-and-after clips are the clearest case: the promise is the edit itself, and the viewer can verify it frame by frame — exactly what a reviewer should do.

video.alt: A tangle of charging cables behind the desk becomes one clipped, labeled setup with a cable organizer kit.
video.label: Cable Organizer Desk Before After
video.caption: Real example: a before/after claim in motion. The tangle becomes the clipped setup on camera — if your clip promises a difference, the difference has to happen in the frame.

sections.h2: Check Your Rights

img.alt: Hands hold plain black travel backpack beside a plain camera and blank phone.

paras: Only photos and logos you own the rights to go into a job. Supplier images need an agreement that covers advertising use. Music comes from the built-in library or tracks you licensed. If a teammate sent the product photo, confirm where it came from before it feeds a paid ad.

sections.h2: Check the Platform Labels

img.alt: Adult hands hold a plain black travel backpack beside a blank laptop and a blank phone.

paras: Each platform sets its own rules for labeling AI-generated content — check the current policy for TikTok, Meta and YouTube before the ad goes live. Two rules are constant everywhere: never present a generated face as a real buyer or reviewer, and never promise health outcomes your product doesn't have.

sections.h2: Fix One Scene or Regenerate the Clip?
paras: A wrong label, a drifting color, an awkward hand: regenerate just that scene with a sharper reference photo and keep the rest. A wrong script, a wrong language, a wrong product: regenerate the whole clip from a better brief.
Failed jobs return their credits, so a rerun never costs extra — the only real cost is the minute you spend writing a clearer description.

sections.h2: How Teams Run the Check

An agency keeps this checklist in the client's onboarding doc and archives each approved file in the library with the version that shipped.

sections.h2: What This Guide Covers
paras: This guide walks the model photo workflow: which source photo works, how to pick and keep a model, and how one garment photo becomes a whole set — model shots, lifestyle scenes and video. Two real clips generated on this site show what a finished set looks like in motion.
By the end you'll know how to launch an entire color set in one afternoon, and what to check before each photo goes live.

sections.h2: Your Clothes on a Model, Without the Shoot

img.alt: Adult man with short silver hair wearing a plain gray hoodie outside a storefront.

paras: The [model photos](/ai-image-generation/model-photos) tool turns a flat-lay or hanger shot into a model photo. Choose the model, the pose and the background; the generator drapes your garment and keeps its color, print and visible details.
Each photo costs 24 credits, the cost shows before the job starts, and failed jobs return their credits.

sections.h2: Start From a Flat Lay or Hanger Shot

img.alt: Hands smooth a plain gray hoodie beside a wooden hanger on a light surface.

paras: One clear photo of the garment is enough: daylight, full front, laid flat or on a hanger. Smooth the wrinkles first — folds in the source photo become folds on the model. Make sure the collar, the cuffs and the hem are fully in frame.
Read every label before upload: the generator reproduces what it sees, including the care tag hanging out of the collar.

sections.h2: Pick the Model and Keep the Face
paras: Choose from 53 AI actors across five age ranges and 31 scenes. Save the model you like and reuse the same face on every product page, marketplace and social post — the collection reads as one brand, not a collage.
Jewelry and eyewear follow the same path: clear close-ups, count the stones, check the clasps. The saved face works across accessories too.

sections.h2: Show the Fit, the Drape, the Fabric
paras: A model photo has to show how the garment sits. The fit check is the standard format — and it works just as well generated as filmed, straight from the garment photo you already have.

video.alt: A short-haired creator shows off a washed-graphic cotton tee in her bedroom: fit check, fabric close-up, tucked and untucked styling, ending on her cart link.
video.label: Washed Graphic Tee Fit Check
video.caption: Real example: a fit check from one garment photo. Watch the beats — the mirror check, the fabric close-up, tucked and untucked — that turn one photo into a whole set of posts.

sections.h2: Build the Whole Color Set Together

img.alt: Adult East Asian man checking the sleeve and hem of a plain gray hoodie in a fitting room.

paras: Run every colorway on the same model and the same scene: the set looks intentional, and shoppers compare colors instead of comparing photos. Generate the white-background main image for the marketplace, the model photo for the page, and the lifestyle shot for social — all from the same garment photo.
If the print drifted or the collar shape changed, rerun with a sharper source photo instead of shipping a version that doesn't match.

sections.h2: Style It More Than One Way
paras: One garment, two outfits doubles the feed without a second garment: the same knit worn open over a tee, then belted, keeps the model and the room identical while the look changes.

video.alt: In front of a full-length mirror she styles a cream chunky-knit cardigan two ways: open over a tee, then belted.
video.label: Cream Chunky Cardigan Two Ways
video.caption: Real example: one garment, two outfits. Open over a tee, then belted — styling variety from a single source photo, with the same model kept across both looks.
